title: Why divide by the shuffles
question: How do you count the ways to choose k things from n when order does not matter?
hook: Deal yourself five cards and the order never matters, so counting hands means undoing all the shuffles.
idea: Count the ordered picks, then divide by the number of orders that give the same group.

beats.prompt: A bowl holds an apple, an orange and a pear. You take two pieces, and now you may take two of the same kind. How many extra choices appear?

choices.label: None; the same choices are still available
choices.feedback: The bowl is unchanged, which makes this tempting, but taking a matching pair is a new choice.

choices.label: Three: two apples, two oranges or two pears
Six: each fruit paired with each other fruit again
choices.feedback: Mixed pairs were already allowed; only the matching pairs are new.

beats.explain: Allowing repeats adds exactly one new choice per kind of fruit: two apples, two oranges and two pears.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of the argument for the combination formula in order
items: Write out all n! permutations of the whole set
Take the first k elements of each permutation as a group
Notice that many permutations give the same group
Divide to remove those duplicate selections
beats.explain: Each permutation gives a group by taking its first k elements, but reordering within the first k or within the last n minus k gives the same group, so you divide.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it means
pairs: a combination in which repetition is allowed
sequences that give the same combination
the number of five-card poker hands
beats.explain: The formula counts ordered picks on top and divides by the orders that give the same group; the poker hand count is the standard example.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A poker hand is a choice of 5 different cards from 52.
The order the cards are held in does not matter.
Two hands with the same cards in different orders are the same hand.
So the number of hands equals the number of ordered sequences of 5 cards, with nothing divided out.
beats.explain: Ordered sequences count each hand once per order of its cards, so that count must be divided by the orders that give the same combination.
